Md Noor, with Omar Sadat, Advocates—For the Petitioners in both the Rules. 
MA Rahim Bhuiyan, Assistant Attorney-General— For the Respondent No. 3.
parties:
Obaidul Karim (Md.) ------ Petitioner [In WP No. 2058 of 2009]
Arjuda Karim   ------ Petitioner [In WP No. 2059 of 2009]

Government of Bangladesh & others ------ Respondents [In both the Rules)
full_judgment:
4. The respondent No. 3 entered appearance through the learned Assistant Attorney General and contested the Rule by filing affidavit-in-opposition denying the material allegations made in the two writ petitions contending inter alia that Annexure-A dated 5-2-2009 clearly shows that the petitioners concealed the particulars of income in their returns submitted for the respective years and the said memos are self contained memos showing definite information in the hands of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes and also obtaining written approval of the Additional Commissioner of Taxes, as required under section 93(2) of the Ordinance. Thus having complied with all the requirements of law the issuance of the impugned memos and the initiation of the proceedings under section 93 are very much lawful. By filing supplementary-affidavits-in-opposition in both the writ petitions the said respondent No. 3 annexed copies of the proposal dated 25-1-2009 seeking approval of re-opening the cases against both the petitioners and also the copies of the approval given thereto by the Additional Commissioner of Taxes on 25-1-2009 (Annexures-1 and 2 to the supplementary-affidavit-in-opposition). Accordingly the said respondent prayed for discharging both the Rules. 

 5. Mr Md Noor, the learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the petitioners in both the Rules, submits that the impugned memos dated 5-2-2009, Annexure-A and the notices, Annexure-G series (in both the writ petitions) are not at all valid notices under section 93 of the Ordinance as the pre-requisites, as specified in section 93 read with section 77(2) have not been complied with. In elaborating his submissions Mr Noor contended that section 77(2) provides that the assessee is to be given not less than 21 days time, to submit his return before proceeding with re-assessment and determine such evasion or escaped assessment, if any, under section 93. In this respect he relied on the case of Commissioner of Income Tax vs Ekbal & Co, reported in Income Tax Report (Bombay High Court) (1945) Vol. XII ITR page-154. Again relying on the case of Tonsukhrai Bodulal vs Income Tax Officer reported in (1962) Vol 46 ITR 325, Mr Noor submits that the issuance of a valid notice under section 34 (which is corresponding to section 93 of the present law) is not merely a procedural requirement but is a condition precedent for the exercise of the jurisdiction of the Income Tax Officer for re-assessing the assessee under the said section. Referring to the language used in Annexure 'A'  “ অর্থাৎ আপনি ২০০২-২০০৩ করবর্ষ হইতে ২০০৭-২০০৮ করবর্ষের জন্য দাখিলকৃত সম্পদ বিবরনীতে উক্ত অপ্রদর্শিত সম্পদ গোপন করিয়াছেন এবং উক্ত গোপনকৃত সম্পদের উপর প্রযোজ্য আয়কর ফাকি দিয়াছেন প্রতীয়মান হইতেছে।” Mr Noor submits that in Annexure 'A' there is no discloser about definite information as to evasion/non discloser of any statement in possession of the DCT nor there is any indication that any prior approval has been obtained from the concerned authority, before issuing such notices as prescribed in the statute. Rather the said Annexure clearly shows “এমতাবস্থায় আপনার ২০০২-২০০৩ করবর্ষ হইতে ২০০৭-২০০৮ করবর্ষের আয়কর মামলা আয়কর অধ্যাদেশ ১৯৮৪ এর ৯৩ ধারায় পুনঃউন্মেচনযোগ্য এবং এই ইউনিটের নথি নং এল (জি) ১৬৩ ২০০৮-২০০৯ তাং ২০০৯ মোতাবেক অনুমোদন সাপেক্ষে পুনঃউন্মেচন করা হইয়াছে।” meaning "subject to approval" the notice appears to have been issued without obtaining the prior approval which is the pre requisite of issuance of notice under section 93. Mr Noor, upon drawing our attention to the blank column of the memo number and date in the said impugned letters submits that Annexure-A does not show that the requirement of sub section 2 of section 93 has been fulfilled. As such the said notices are not sustainable in the eye of law. Referring to Annexure-G series, the Income Tax form IT -90, used for issuing notice under section 93 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984, he submits that although the authority has mentioned the assessment year and filled up the other particulars of the said form by hand and upon putting a tick mark on serial No. 1 showing “কর নির্ধারন এড়াইয়া গিয়াছে” but upon drawing our attention to the opposite page of the said notice, Mr. Noor submits, that the authority upon striking out the printed words "within 35 days" has put "within 21 days" by hand. Meaning to submit return "within 21 days of receipt of this notice" for the assessment year mentioned on the first page. Accordingly, Mr Noor submits that when section 93(1) specifically provides that the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes may issue a notice to the assessee containing all or any of the requirements which may be included in a notice under section 77 and may proceed in accordance with law, the time specified in the impugned notices being less than the statutory period of "not being less than twenty one days" as prescribed in section 77(2) of the Ordinance 1984, the said notice is without lawful authority such the same are void. Apart from the above, Mr Noor submits that both Annexure A and Annexure-G series, which the authority claims to be the statutory notice under section 93, are not at all notices in the eye of law as the requirements of law as provided for in sections 93(1), 93(2) and section 77 are absent in the said notices. He submits, on the contrary, Annexure-A, in Writ Petition Nos. 2058 of 2009, clearly shows that the space for putting the date and number of the prior approval being kept vacant and by using the words “ অনুমোদন সাপেক্ষে" meaning "subject to approval", in Annexure-A the said annexure clearly shows that no prior approval has ever been obtained. Thus under all circumstances the impugned Annexures- A and G series are void. 

 6. Mr Noor further submits that the allegation as to some assets having not been shown in the wealth statement filed by the petitioner with specifications is vague. As such non mention of any definite particular as to which assets have not been shown therein, the Annexure-A has fallen short of reconciling the deficiency of the notice, as required under section 93 of the Ordinance, 1984. Accordingly to him, assets shown or not shown in the wealth statement are not income as such not chargeable to tax. Again referring to the term, “প্রতীয়মান হইতেছে” used in the said notice, he submits that the meaning of the meaning of the same is " appear to be" which does not, under any circumstances, discloses that there are "definite information" in possession of DCT. Thus from the above contentions Annexure-A cannot ever be termed as a good notice with definite information, as to evasion of Tax, in the possession of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes. Thus he submits that in the absence of (i) previous approval obtained from the Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes; (ii) definite information in possession of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes and (iii) clear twenty one days time having not been given; the impugned memo, Annexure-A, and Annexure-G series are nothing but some papers containing some statements based on surmise and conjecture on the basis of which file of an assessee, which has been closed finally after due consideration by the authority, cannot be re-opened under Section 93. On the question of definite information Mr. Noor cited a decision of the Tribunal, which though do not have any binding effect upon this Court but can be taken into consideration as an accepted principle, as decided by the superior Court of the country. Accordingly, referring to Income Tax Appeals No. 1125, 1126 and 1127 of 1958-59 of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, reported in 4 Taxation (1961) 94 he submits that definite information and previous approval of the Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes being conspicuously absent in the body of the notices purportedly issued under section 93 of the Ordinance, Annexures-A and G series cannot be said to be a valid notice. 

 7. Lastly, Mr Noor submits that section 93(3)(c) provides general limitation of two years for issuance of notice under section 93(1). But section 93(3)(b) makes an exception to the said limitation providing five years from the end of the assessment year for re-opening the file of an assessee on the ground of concealment of particulars of income, furnishing inaccurate particulars or omitted/failed to disclose all material facts necessary for the assessment for such year. He submits that in the present case the impugned Annexures A and G series contain that the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes (DCT) believes that income, chargeable to tax, has escaped assessment. This does not mean that the petitioners concealed any particular of their income, which is a condition precedent for re-opening the file within the extended period of five years time from the end of the assessment year as provided for in clause 93(3)(b). Thus he submits that such expression of concealment being absent in the body of Annexure-G and the particulars given in Annexure-A not being definite information and prior approval having not been obtained the notice issued on 5-2-2009 (Annexure-A) as well as Annexure-G are statutorily barred by limitation and are not valid notices in the eye of law. 

 8. In respect of Writ Petition Nos. 2059 of 2009 Mr Noor reiterated all the submissions made hereinabove on all the points except the Memo number regarding obtaining previous approval of the designated authority as shown in Annexure-A. Referring to paragraph containing previous approval as shown in Annexure-A he submits that the same appears to have been obtained vide Memo dated 25-1-2009 and the so called approval appears to have been sought to and obtained from the Additional Commissioner of Taxes as appears from Annexures 1 and 2 appended to the supplementary-affidavit-filed by Respondent No. 3 which is not at all an approval under section 93(2) as the law provides that the same has to be obtained from the Inspecting Joint commissioner of Taxes not Additional Commissioner of Taxes. Mr Noor further submits that though Annexure-A contains allegations that the petitioner has escaped paying tax for the assessment years 2003-2004 to 2007-2008 but Annexure-G 5, the so called statutory notice under form IT-90 issued under section 93, clearly shows that payment of tax alleged to have been escaped for the assessment years 2002-2003 (not 2003-2004) which is contrary to Annexure A as admittedly no allegation of evading tax for the assessment year 2002-2003 has been made in Annexure-A. Moreover, in some of the notices (Annexure-G series) the petitioner has been directed to submit return under 93 within 21 days upon striking out the printed words within 35 days, but in some of the notices 35 days has not been struck down nor any date/time has been mentioned. Thus the notices under Annexure-G series are not only contradictory to each other but the same are also clear reflection of non application of mind. As such re opening of the file of the assessee under section 93 for all those years mentioned therein specially for the assessment years 2002-2003 is not at all tenable in the eye of law. As such, under no circumstances the impugned notices can be deemed to have been issued in accordance with and in compliance of law i.e. section 93(2) read with section 77 of the Ordinance. 

 9. On the other hand, Mr MA Rahim Bhuiyan, the learned Assistant Attorney General appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 3 submits that for re opening the case of an assessee under section 93, admittedly, three elements, specifically prescribed in sections 93(1) and (2) of the Ordinance 1984 are essential; those are (i) definite information in possession of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes; (ii) prior approval of the designated authority and (iii) not less than 21 days time to be given in the notice. Accordingly, he submits that although Annexure-G series dated 21-5-2009 are the printed notices but there is no such column for explaining about the definite information in possession of the DCT and also about prior approval of the designated authority, in the said notices. That is why Annexure-A has been issued upon both the assessees describing about the information of escaping assessment and the manner of escaping the same and also about obtaining prior approval of the designated authority, along with Annexure-G. He submits that the requirements, as to allowing time as contemplated in section 93(1) read with section 77(2) of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984 has been fulfilled in Annexure-G series. So Annexures-A and G are to be construed together for the purpose of validity of issuance of the notice under section 93. He submits that on perusal of the contents of Annexure-A it will be clear that the petitioners did not disclose about the bank interest, bank balance, purchase of share and investment by purchasing flat in a specific assessment year in their respective returns and hereby they escaped assessment. So the requirement as to definite information is very much in possession of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes. 

 10. On the second requirement regarding obtaining prior approval he submits that the authority, on 25-1-2009 gave approval which has been incorporated in Annexure-A to Writ Petition Nos. 2059 of 2009 but inadvertently the said memo number and the date has not been incorporated in Annexure-A to the Writ Petition Nos. 2058 of 2009. However, referring to Annexures-1 and 2 to the supplementary-affidavit-in-opposition, Mr. Bhuiyan submits that Annexure-1 is the proposal for approval to re open the case of the petitioners addressed to the higher authority and Annexure-2 is the approval given by the higher authority on the same day. Thus, the preconditions, as contemplated in section 93(2), have been duly com-plied with. On the question of third requirement as to giving 21 days time by striking out 35 days in the 2nd page of the Annexure-G series, he submits that apparently it show that the assessees were directed to file their respective returns under section 93, within 21 days, but he frankly admits that the law provides for, 'not being less than 21 days' and, as such, he cannot deny the fact of allowing less then 21 days time upon striking out the printed figure 35 days. He submits that it is a bonafide mistake which, under no circumstances, will prejudice the petitioners. Rather such error will not vitiate the notice, as contemplated in section 179 of the Ordinance. Accordingly, he submits that such error, defect or omission being not substantial in nature for prejudicing the assessee the same can not be a ground for declaring the notice invalid or illegal. 

 11. In reply to one of the submissions of Mr Noor as to no provision for payment of tax on the wealth and thus, allegation of evading tax on the wealth, as shown in the petitions returns, as alleged in Annexure-A will not in any way bring the petitioners within the mischief of evasion of Tax Mr. Bhuiyan submits that section 19 of the Income Tax Ordinance clearly provides that unexplained investment is to be deemed as an income from other sources and, as such, the petitioners without showing the aforesaid investment, as income, in the wealth statement, the allegation of escaping/ evading tax is very much justifiable. On the question of limitation Mr Bhuiyan submits that the law is very clear in this respect. Section 93(3) (b) clearly contemplated that in case the assessee concealed the particulars of his income or furnished inaccurate particulars thereof or omitted or failed to disclose all material facts necessary for the assessment for any assessment year then the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes within five years from the end of the assessment year may issue notice under section 93. In the instant case, according to Mr Bhuiyan, the allegation of concealment, non furnishing and non-disclosing the material facts has been made against the petitioners and the same being very much within five years of the assessment year is permissible in law. 

 12. On the question of approval by the designated authority, Mr Bhuiyan referred to sections 3(3A) and 4 read with section 2(36) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984. He submits that section 3(3A) provides that the Additional Commissioner of Taxes, may be either Appellate Additional Commissioner of Taxes or Inspecting Additional Commissioner of Taxes, and under sub section 4 the legislature provides that Joint Commissioner of Taxes, may be either Appellate Joint Commissioner of taxes or Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes. Then referring to section 2(36) he submits that 'Inspecting Joint Commissioner' means a person appointed to be an Inspecting Additional Commissioner of Taxes under section 3 and includes an Inspecting Additional Commissioner of Taxes and also a person appointed to hold current charge of an Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes. Thus he submits that the Additional Commissioner of Taxes, who gave the approval in the present case, being the Additional Commissioner, he may either be the Additional Appellate Commissioner or Inspecting Additional Commissioner of Taxes. Thus he submits that since Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes includes Inspecting Additional Commissioner of Taxes and since Additional Commissioner of Taxes may be Inspecting Additional Commissioner of Taxes so the approval given by the Additional Commissioner of Taxes is a proper approval under the law as contemplated in section 93(2) read with sub section 3, (3A) and 4 read with section 2(36) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984. Hence both the Rules are liable to be discharged with costs. 

 13. Upon hearing the learned Advocates for both the parties it appears that the questions raised in these two Rules are: (i) whether the pre-requisites as contemplated in section 93(2) as to definite information in the possession of the DCT and obtaining prior approval of the appropriate authority and in this regard who is the appropriate authority to accord prior approval; (ii) whether 21 days clear time as required under section 77(2) has been given; and (iii) whether allegations brought in a separate memo, namely, Annexure-A, specifying the fact that the notice, as claimed by the authority, is a statutory notice under section 93 of the Ordinance, 1984 to substantiate Annexure-G series and what are the particulars to be incorporated in the said notice or memo (Annexure G series). On perusal of Annexure-G series it appears that the authority has printed IT-90 form, (Annexure-G series), describing it to be a notice under section 93. But on a query, the learned Assistant Attorney-General could not give any satisfactory reply as to the statutory basis of such printed form i.e. IT-90 or issuance of separate memo vide Annexure A. Mr Bhuiyan handed over the Income Tax Manual printed by the Bangladesh Government Press in 1980 under the Income Tax Act 1922 wherein section 34 (corresponding to section 93 of the present Ordinance), provides for a printed notice and Annexure-G series is described by the learned Assistant Attorney-General to be the Bengali version of the said notice under section 93. Upon going through the present Ordinance and the previous Act of 1922, it appears that section 185 gives power to the Board to make Rules on respective matters. Accordingly, having gone through the Rules we do not find any prescribed form of notice to be issued under section 34 or under section 93. Thus it can be construed that the authority, for their own conveniences adopted particular forms for particular section. Accordingly, IT Form 90 has been incorporated which is also being used for section 93 of the present Ordinance. In this respect the respondents could not produce any authority. On perusal of several decisions referred to by the learned Advocates it appears that on similar situation when notice under section 34 of the Indian Income Tax Act 1922 was issued in the same form, IT-90, as of the present case and if the language of such notices clinches the matter against the department to the effect that only one printed form was issued in which no distinction was made whether the notice was issued in consequence of 'definite information' or otherwise such notices were construed to have been issued not on the basis of 'definite information'. The said view having been consistent and not been varied in any other forum the same remains to be an acceptable principle. On perusal of the printed notice IT-90 form (Annexure-G), it appears that there is no scope of making any reference as to such pre requisites, in the said form as contemplated in section 93(2). Thus the IT form (IT 90) printed under the Income Tax Manual, clearly shows that the authority used the said form only for the purpose of their administrative conveniences, not as a requirement of law. Thus, the said printed notice being not in accordance with the requirement of the statute and there being no scope of showing possession of any definite information and/or obtaining prior approval of the Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes, the said notices under IT 90 form, Annexure-G series, so long being used by the department can only be said to be not in accordance with law. 

 14. Now, let us turn to Annexure-A, by which the learned Assistant Attorney-General claims that the requirement of section 93(2) has been fulfilled. From the said annexure it appears that in the first page the authority alleged that in the concerned returns there is no disclosure as to bank accounts, interest and purchase of certain properties as such the petitioners have evaded Tax. The said Annexure-A also contains a paragraph as to obtaining prior approval from the higher authority. But the same does not reflect that the requirement of section 93(2) read with section 77(2) of the Ordinance has been complied with. According to Mr Bhuiyan reading Annexures-'A' and 'G' series together will show that the requirements of the statutory notice under section 93 has been prima facie complied with. But question comes whether definite information as alleged in Annexure-A, are really definite in nature and weather the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes is in possession of such information and whether prior approval has been obtained from the authority as designated under the law. 

 16. On the other hand, considering Annexures "A" and "G" series together let us see whether the pre requirement of section 93(2) as to obtaining prior approval can be construed to have been obtained. In the last but one paragraph of Annexure 'A' no number and date of any memo has been given by which it can be construed that such approval has been obtained prior to issuance of the said Annexures. Moreover, by using the words “অনুমোদন সাপেক্ষে” (which means "subject to approval") in the said annexure it is clear that the authority did not obtain any prior approval. As such the pre requirement of the statute does not appear to have been fulfilled. If we consider the term "subject to approval", means "approval has been obtained" as submitted by Mr Bhuiyan, even then we need to see as to who has given such approval. On perusal of Annexures-1 and 2 to the supplementary-affidavit-in-opposition it appears that the proposal has been made by the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, Audit Wing, LTU, Dhaka on 25-1-2009 to re-open the files of the petitioners purportedly under section 93 of the said Ordinance to the Additional Commissioner (LTU), Dhaka, and pursuant to the said proposal the Additional Commissioner of Taxes (LTU) Dhaka has given such approval in writing on 25-1-2009 in respect of re-opening the files of the petitioners under section 93 (Annexure-2). For the purpose of deciding whether the said approval is a valid one let us see the requirement of section 93(2) which reads as follows:— 

 "93(2). No proceeding under sub-section (1) shall be initiated unless definite information has come into the possession of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes [and he has obtained] the previous approval of the Inspecting Joint Commissioner in writing to do so, except in a case where a return has not been filed under sections 75 or 77." 

 17. From the above provision it appears that the statute has given specific authority to the "Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes" to give such prior approval in writing. According to Mr. Bhuiyan the Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes is the designated authority to give such approval as such the approval given by the Additional Commissioner of Taxes is a valid approval since the Additional Commissioner of Taxes may also act as Inspecting Additional Commissioner, as described under sections 3, (3A) and section 2(36) and therefore, the Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes must mean and include Inspecting Additional Commissioner of Taxes and also a person appointed to hold current charge of Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes. We can not agree with the contention of Mr. Bhuiyan, because although section 3(3A) provides that Additional Commissioner of Taxes may be either Appellate Additional Commissioner of Taxes or Inspecting Additional Commissioner of Taxes and Section 2(36) provides that Inspecting Joint Commissioner means a person appointed to be an Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes under section 3 that includes an Inspecting Additional Commissioner of Taxes. But none of the aforesaid provisions provide Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes would mean and include Additional Commissioner of Taxes (LTU). Now if we again look at the impugned annexures we find that the authority, who alleged to have given the approval appears to be "Additional Commissioner (LTU) Dhaka", who may either be "Inspecting Additional Commissioner" but does not include and mean "Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes". Section 2(36) in its clearest terms described that the "Inspecting Joint Commissioner" means and includes Inspecting Additional Commissioner, not "Additional Commissioner". Thus under no circumstances the Additional Commissioner (LTU) Dhaka, who alleged to have approved the proposal of issuing notice under section 93 in the present case, can be contemplated as "Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes". Moreover, the authority who alleged to have accorded approval appears to be Additional Commissioner of Taxes (LTU) who holds a different office of Large Taxpayers Unit not an Additional Commissioner as submitted by Mr. Bhuiyan. According to the provision of law an "Inspecting Joint Commissioner" of Taxes includes an "Inspecting Additional Commissioner". Thus, the alleged approval granted by Annexure "2" being signed by the "Additional Commissioner (LTU)" not the "Inspecting Joint Commissioner" the same is not an appropriate order of approval within the meaning of section 93(2) of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984. The affidavit-in-opposition also does not contain any averment or material to show that the "Additional Commissioner of Taxes who alleged to have accorded the approval, was entrusted with the current charge of "Inspecting Joint Commissioner" of Taxes, who under the law could accord approval for re-opening the case of the petitioners. 

 20. In the case of Commissioner of Income Tax vs Ekbal & Co, reported in (1945) XIII ITR 154; Tonsukhrai Bodulal vs Income Tax Officer reported in (1962) XLVI Income Tax Reports 325 and in the case of Department vs Assessee reported in (1961) Vol. IV Taxation 94 (Trib), it appears that the consistent finding of the jurists are "the word " definite information" were conspicuously absent in the body of the printed form under section 34 of the Income Tax Act. There being no distinction in the printed form whether the notice was issued in consequence of 'definite information' or otherwise it cannot be held that the notices were issued on the basis of definite information and since the notices initiating proceedings under section 34 were not in pursuance of definite information and since previous approval in writing of the Inspecting Joint Commissioner, which is essential condition conferring jurisdiction on the Income Tax Officer to initiate proceedings for reassessment in cases other than in which notices are issued on definite information was also absent, the Income Tax Officer had no jurisdiction to issue notice and, as such, the reassessment proceedings were legally void." In the present case definite information as to evasion of tax in possession of the Deputy Commission of Taxes as well as prior approval of the Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes along with clear 21 days notice time being absent the impugned notices cannot be treated as valid notices under section 93 of the Ordinance. 

 22. Having gone through the provisions of Section 34 of the Income Tax Act 1922 and section 93(2) of the present Ordinance we find that the legislature has intentionally inserted the provisions in the present law in place of the words used in the earlier law for the purpose of issuing of a valid statutory notice in respect of definite information in possession of the DCT and prior approval to be obtained from the designated authority, namely, the Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes upon repealing the earlier provision "to obtain approval from either of the two designated officers" therein. In the present Ordinance the law has been made a mandatory provision, giving specific authority to the "Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes" only, to accord prior approval. When statute provides something in plain and simple language, there cannot be any ambiguity or other implication. Thus when section 93 clearly provides for obtaining prior approval of the "Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes" there cannot be any other authority to give such approval. So, prior approval from the authority designated in the statute is a must, which is the pre condition of such notice. This view finds support in the case of Abu Bakar Siddique vs Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed 49 DLR 1. In the case of tribal Hasan Mahmud vs Bangladesh, 60 DLR 88 it has been held that every word of the statute should be given proper attention for harmonious discrimination interpretation of the intention of the legislature. Apart from the above the accepted principle of law is once returns are accepted by the authority certifying that the returns are in order, unless found definite, the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes is not competent to serve notice upon the petitioner under section 93 asking him to submit fresh return holding the returns already assessed and accepted as under assessed, as has been decided in the case of American Express Bank Ltd vs Chairman National Board of Revenue reported in 54 DLR 6. 

 23. Having considered the submissions and discussions made hereinabove we are of the view that Annexure-G series having no support of law the same cannot be termed as a statutory notice though two Annexures A and G reading together may be termed as a notice under section 93 and to that extent the re-opening of the file within five years back from 5-2-2009, the date of notices, may not be barred by limitation. But the notice for assessment years 2002-2003 and 2003-2004 are definitely barred by limitation as those are beyond the five years period from 5-2-2009. So far the notices for assessment years 2004-2005 to 2007-08, are concerned, though the same are within five years from 5-2-2009 but for the reasons stated hereinabove, particularly for failure to prove obtaining prior approval from the designated authority, namely, the "Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes", and failure to prove of having definite information in possession of the DCT and also "Not less than 21 days" statutory time having not been allowed, the notices for the said assessment years are invalid and beyond the scope of law and, as such, not valid notices under section 93 of the Act.
